newsitem.title: USA: US utility customers still clamor for lower costs.
newsitem.headline: US utility customers still clamor for lower costs.

text.p: Moves to deregulate U.S. natural gas and electric markets have roused consumer hopes for lower energy costs, but some critics say cheaper rates have been slow in coming.
While unbundling sales and transmission services and more customer choice have stirred competition, some energy users said the benefits have yet to filter downstream.

"If choice is here, it's in disguise because I don't recognize it. We're seeking more competitive rates, but some utilities have decided to forego change until its forced upon them," Birmingham Steel chairman Robert Garvey told the American Gas Association Bankers Conference Wednesday.
Garvey said the regulated mindset of utilities was making it more difficult for industrial customers to compete.

"Utilities will only move off the dime if we have a viable option. Where we're getting stonewalled, we're looking at installing our own gas turbines," he said, noting a lot of steel mills were locating plants near transmission lines.
In the end, Garvey said, it may take federal regulations to completely unbundle services and create a more level playing field.
"What's unbundled when the utility owns the marketing company?" he said, adding there have been marked reductions in the cost of gas but rates from local distribution companies were still too high.

While marketers conceded the industry was still in the process of adjusting to rapid change, they said the keys to success in a newly deregulated world were efficiency and a clear focus on the customer.
And most agreed the rapid pace of strategic alliances and mergers would continue, as companies scrambled to gain an edge on the competition.

"We're seeking better ways of doing business. The challenge is putting together structures to implement change with an emphasis on customer needs," said William Heil, president of All Energy Marketing, an Eastern Enterprises unit in Boston.
Meanwhile, suppliers will continue to look for ways to control costs, reduce rates and develop a wider array of services that go beyond just providing a commodity like gas or electricity.

"We're doing everything we can to control costs so we can provide shippers with rate reductions in the future," said Robert Evans, marketing vice president at Panenergy unit Texas Eastern Transmission Corp.
"Customers more and more will focus on price, and getting costs down will be absolutely paramount," Laurence Downes, chairman of New Jersey Resources, said.
